Imitate Paul only as he imitates Christ (verse 1)

Henry believes this opening verse properly belongs with the previous chapter's conclusion.

Paul preached teachings the Corinthians ought to believe, but also lived in a way they ought to follow.

Nevertheless, Christ is our perfect example.

We should imitate the actions of human beings described in Scripture only insofar as those actions resemble Christ's.

Order and appropriate dress in worship (verses 2–16)

Paul now begins considering abuses in public Christian gatherings, a subject continued in chapter 14.

Corinthian believers had received many spiritual gifts but had fallen into serious mistakes in using them.

As Christ did the Father's will and sought God's glory, Christians must openly acknowledge their submission to Christ and seek his honor.

Even our clothing and outward conduct should avoid bringing dishonor upon him.

Henry teaches that the woman was created to assist and comfort the man, and therefore should not conduct herself in public worship as if claiming independence from the order God appointed.

He interprets “power” on the woman's head as a veil, worn because of the angels who are present as witnesses of worship.

Their presence should restrain believers from misconduct in the assembly.

Yet Henry immediately adds that man and woman were created for one another.

They ought to bring mutual comfort and blessing, not live as a slave and a tyrant.

God's ordering of leadership and submission, both in Providence and in grace, aims at mutual assistance and benefit.

In the churches of that time, women commonly attended and participated in public worship wearing veils, and Henry considers it right that they did so.

Christianity generally permits a nation's social customs when they do not contradict truth and holiness.

It does not endorse deliberate eccentricity merely for the sake of appearing different.

Divisions and selfishness at the Lord's table (verses 17–22)

Paul rebuked abuses of the Lord's Supper.

When ordinances do not help people grow spiritually, they may instead harden them.

Corinthian gatherings were marked by divisions and disputes.

People can worship in separate congregations while still loving one another.

They can also remain together in the same congregation while behaving without love.

Henry judges that this lack of charity is the more serious kind of schism.

An unworthy and careless way of receiving the Supper adds guilt.

Some wealthy Corinthians treated poorer Christians shamefully during the meal or accompanying love feast.

They consumed the food they had brought before poorer members could share it.

Some remained hungry while others had more than enough.

What ought to have strengthened fellowship became a cause of division.

Avoid any conduct that dishonors the sacred meal.

We may not commonly turn it into an occasion of gluttony now.

But do we sometimes turn it into a support for self-righteous pride or a cover for hypocrisy?

Do not rest in outward forms of worship.

Examine the heart.

Christ's institution and proper reception of the Supper (verses 23–34)

Paul knew the Lord's Supper through revelation from Christ.

Its visible signs are bread and wine.

The food eaten is still called bread even when Christ calls it his body.

Henry understands this as clear evidence that the bread is not literally transformed into flesh.

Matthew records Christ commanding the disciples all to drink from the cup (Matthew 26:27).

Henry takes this wording as opposing the withholding of the cup from any believer.

These outward signs represent Christ's body broken and blood shed, along with every blessing flowing from his death and atoning sacrifice.

Christ took bread and cup, gave thanks, broke the bread and distributed both bread and cup.

Believers are to take, eat and drink, doing so in remembrance of him.

Yet the visible actions are not the whole or even the principal part of the ordinance.

The believer must receive Christ as Lord and Life, surrender to him and draw nourishment from him through faith.

The Supper remembers Christ dying for us and Christ now interceding at God's right hand on the basis of his sacrifice.

It also celebrates God's grace in our redemption.

We declare that Christ's death is our life, the source of hope and spiritual comfort.

We proclaim his death and plead it as the accepted sacrifice and ransom.

This ordinance was not appointed for only a few years.

It continues as part of the church's life.

Paul then warns against receiving it with a corrupt attitude, maintaining fellowship with sin and death while claiming to renew covenant fellowship with God.

Such hypocrisy is seriously guilty and may lead to divine judgment.

But the warning must not discourage genuine believers who fear their own weakness from attending the Supper.

The Holy Spirit did not cause this passage to be written to frighten sincere Christians away from their duty.

Satan has often misused it for precisely that purpose.

Paul was speaking to believers and warning them about temporal judgments through which God disciplined his offending servants.

In judgment, God remembers mercy.

He often corrects those he loves.

It is better to endure suffering now than to remain miserable forever.

Therefore self-examination is necessary for a right approach to the Lord's table.

If we examine ourselves thoroughly, condemn what is sinful and correct our ways, we may avoid divine discipline.

Paul concludes by warning them not to repeat the disordered practices that brought dishonor upon the Supper.

May our worship never become an occasion for provoking the Lord's judgment.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.11.1]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
The apostle, after an exhortation to follow him,
(1)
corrects some abuses.
(2-16)
Also contentions, divisions, and disorderly celebrations of the Lord's supper. | (17-22) |
He reminds them of the nature and design of its institution. | (23-26) |
And directs how to attend upon it in a due manner. | (27-34) |
Verse 1
The first verse of this chapter seems properly to be the close to the last. The apostle not only preached such doctrine as they ought to believe, but led such a life as they ought to live. Yet Christ being our perfect example, the actions and conduct of men, as related in the Scriptures, should be followed only so far as they are like to his.
[1Cor.11.2-1Cor.11.16]
Verses 2-16
Here begin particulars respecting the public assemblies, ch. 1Co 14. In the abundance of spiritual gifts bestowed on the Corinthians, some abuses had crept in; but as Christ did the will, and sought the honour of God, so the Christian should avow his subjection to Christ, doing his will and seeking his glory. We should, even in our dress and habit, avoid every thing that may dishonour Christ. The woman was made subject to man, because made for his help and comfort. And she should do nothing, in Christian assemblies, which looked like a claim of being equal. She ought to have "power," that is, a veil, on her head, because of the angels. Their presence should keep Christians from all that is wrong while in the worship of God. Nevertheless, the man and the woman were made for one another. They were to be mutual comforts and blessings, not one a slave, and the other a tyrant. God has so settled matters, both in the kingdom of providence and that of grace, that the authority and subjection of each party should be for mutual help and benefit. It was the common usage of the churches, for women to appear in public assemblies, and join in public worship, veiled; and it was right that they should do so. The Christian religion sanctions national customs wherever these are not against the great principles of truth and holiness; affected singularities receive no countenance from any thing in the Bible.
[1Cor.11.17-1Cor.11.22]
Verses 17-22
The apostle rebukes the disorders in their partaking of the Lord's supper. The ordinances of Christ, if they do not make us better, will be apt to make us worse. If the use of them does not mend, it will harden. Upon coming together, they fell into divisions, schisms. Christians may separate from each other's communion, yet be charitable one towards another; they may continue in the same communion, yet be uncharitable. This last is schism, rather than the former. There is a careless and irregular eating of the Lord's supper, which adds to guilt. Many rich Corinthians seem to have acted very wrong at the Lord's table, or at the love-feasts, which took place at the same time as the supper. The rich despised the poor, and ate and drank up the provisions they brought, before the poor were allowed to partake; thus some wanted, while others had more than enough. What should have been a bond of mutual love and affection, was made an instrument of discord and disunion. We should be careful that nothing in our behaviour at the Lord's table, appears to make light of that sacred institution. The Lord's supper is not now made an occasion for gluttony or revelling, but is it not often made the support of self-righteous pride, or a cloak for hypocrisy? Let us never rest in the outward forms of worship; but look to our hearts.
[1Cor.11.23-1Cor.11.34]
Verses 23-34
The apostle describes the sacred ordinance, of which he had the knowledge by revelation from Christ. As to the visible signs, these are the bread and wine. What is eaten is called bread, though at the same time it is said to be the body of the Lord, plainly showing that the apostle did not mean that the bread was changed into flesh. St. Matthew tells us, our Lord bid them all drink of the cup, ch. [Matt.26.27] Mt 26:27, as if he would, by this expression, provide against any believer being deprived of the cup. The things signified by these outward signs, are Christ's body and blood, his body broken, his blood shed, together with all the benefits which flow from his death and sacrifice. Our Saviour's actions were, taking the bread and cup, giving thanks, breaking the bread, and giving both the one and the other. The actions of the communicants were, to take the bread and eat, to take the cup and drink, and to do both in remembrance of Christ. But the outward acts are not the whole, or the principal part, of what is to be done at this holy ordinance. Those who partake of it, are to take him as their Lord and Life, yield themselves up to him, and live upon him. Here is an account of the ends of this ordinance. It is to be done in remembrance of Christ, to keep fresh in our minds his dying for us, as well as to remember Christ pleading for us, in virtue of his death, at God's right hand. It is not merely in remembrance of Christ, of what he has done and suffered; but to celebrate his grace in our redemption. We declare his death to be our life, the spring of all our comforts and hopes. And we glory in such a declaration; we show forth his death, and plead it as our accepted sacrifice and ransom. The Lord's supper is not an ordinance to be observed merely for a time, but to be continued. The apostle lays before the Corinthians the danger of receiving it with an unsuitable temper of mind; or keeping up the covenant with sin and death, while professing to renew and confirm the covenant with God. No doubt such incur great guilt, and so render themselves liable to spiritual judgements. But fearful believers should not be discouraged from attending at this holy ordinance. The Holy Spirit never caused this scripture to be written to deter serious Christians from their duty, though the devil has often made this use of it. The apostle was addressing Christians, and warning them to beware of the temporal judgements with which God chastised his offending servants. And in the midst of judgement, God remembers mercy: he many times punishes those whom he loves. It is better to bear trouble in this world, than to be miserable for ever. The apostle points our the duty of those who come to the Lord's table. Self-examination is necessary to right attendance at this holy ordinance. If we would thoroughly search ourselves, to condemn and set right what we find wrong, we should stop Divine judgements. The apostle closes all with a caution against the irregularities of which the Corinthians were guilty at the Lord's table. Let all look to it, that they do not come together to God's worship, so as to provoke him, and bring down vengeance on themselves.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe variety of use of spiritual gifts are shown.1–11In the human body every member has its place and use.12–26This is applied to the church of Christ.27–30And there is something more excellent than spiritual gifts.31
Spiritual gifts serve the church, not personal pride (verses 1–11)

The extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit were powers given during Christianity's first generations, helping convince unbelievers and spread the gospel.

Spiritual gifts and saving grace are very different.

Both are freely given by God.

But grace is given for the salvation of the person receiving it.

Gifts are given for the good and salvation of others.

Someone may therefore possess remarkable gifts without possessing saving grace.

The Corinthians exercised many extraordinary gifts in public gatherings, sometimes making a public display of them while lacking true godliness and Christian love.

Before conversion they had been pagans, not governed by Christ's Spirit.

No one can truly confess Christ as Lord with believing dependence upon him unless the Holy Spirit produces that faith.

Nor could anyone truly believe in their heart, or confirm Christ's message through a miracle, without the Spirit's power.

There are different gifts and offices, but all come from one God, one Lord and one Spirit: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the source of spiritual blessings.

No gift exists merely for the recipient's benefit.

Serving others with a gift makes its use truly fruitful.

Paul's examples include understanding the truths of Christianity clearly, expressing doctrine accurately, knowing mysteries and giving wise guidance.

They also include healing, miracles, a special ability to explain Scripture, and speaking or interpreting languages.

All knowledge of God's truth and all ability to share it must result in glory to God alone.

Indeed, greater gifts create greater temptations to pride.

Those possessing them need more grace to remain humble and spiritually minded, and may undergo more difficult experiences through which God humbles them.

No one has reason to boast about gifts received or despise others who lack them.

Every member contributes to Christ's one body (verses 12–26)

Christ and his church form one body, with Christ as Head and believers as members.

Baptism is a divinely appointed outward ordinance identifying people with this body.

It signifies new birth and is associated with the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5).

But only the Spirit's renewing work, not outward baptism by itself, makes a person a living member of Christ.

Likewise, believers receive strength through fellowship with Christ at the Supper not simply by drinking wine, but by receiving the one Spirit.

Every member of the body has a particular form, position and purpose.

Even a member regarded as insignificant belongs to the body.

Differences among members are necessary.

Christians likewise have different abilities and responsibilities.

We should fulfill the duties of our own positions without resentment, rivalry or complaining.

All the members need one another.

Every member of Christ's body can and ought to be useful to fellow members.

The entire body should be united by the strongest bonds of love.

All its members should seek the good of the whole.

Every Christian depends upon others and ought to give as well as receive help.

How much more the spirit of unity should govern the church!

God appoints different offices and gifts (verses 27–31)

Hatred, jealousy, pride, contempt and quarrels are unnatural among Christians.

They resemble members of the same body fighting or ignoring one another.

Paul condemns the pride and contentiousness with which the Corinthians compared spiritual gifts.

The Holy Spirit appoints different offices and distributes distinct abilities.

Henry describes leading ministers, teachers able to interpret Scripture, others laboring in word and doctrine, workers able to heal sickness, those helping people in weakness, people managing the church's charitable funds and practical administration, and those able to speak different languages.

Notice that speaking languages comes last in this list.

How empty it is to possess this gift merely to entertain people or exalt oneself!

God does not give every gift to every believer.

If he did, the church would cease to have differentiated members, as though a natural body were made entirely of eyes or ears.

The Spirit distributes gifts according to his own will.

Christians must be content when given a less visible responsibility, without despising those with greater abilities.

Likewise, those given more prominent gifts must never despise those with less.

How blessed the church would be if every member faithfully performed the duty assigned!

Instead of seeking the highest status or most impressive gifts, leave the appointment of God's instruments to him.

Final approval will not belong to those who sought the most prominent positions, but to those who faithfully used the trust given them and worked diligently for their Master.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.12.1-1Cor.12.11]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
The variety of use of spiritual gifts are shown. | (1-11) |
In the human body every member has its place and use. | (12-26) |
This is applied to the church of Christ. | (27-30) |
And there is something more excellent than spiritual gifts. | (31) |
Verses 1-11
Spiritual gifts were extraordinary powers bestowed in the first ages, to convince unbelievers, and to spread the gospel. Gifts and graces greatly differ. Both were freely given of God. But where grace is given, it is for the salvation of those who have it. Gifts are for the advantage and salvation of others; and there may be great gifts where there is no grace. The extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit were chiefly exercised in the public assemblies, where the Corinthians seem to have made displays of them, wanting in the spirit of piety, and of Christian love. While heathens, they had not been influenced by the Spirit of Christ. No man can call Christ Lord, with believing dependence upon him, unless that faith is wrought by the Holy Ghost. No man could believe with his heart, or prove by a miracle, that Jesus was Christ, unless by the Holy Ghost. There are various gifts, and various offices to perform, but all proceed from one God, one Lord, one Spirit; that is, from the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, the origin of all spiritual blessings. No man has them merely for himself. The more he profits others, the more will they turn to his own account. The gifts mentioned appear to mean exact understanding, and uttering the doctrines of the Christian religion; the knowledge of mysteries, and skill to give advice and counsel. Also the gift of healing the sick, the working of miracles, and to explain Scripture by a peculiar gift of the Spirit, and ability to speak and interpret languages. If we have any knowledge of the truth, or any power to make it known, we must give all the glory of God. The greater the gifts are, the more the possessor is exposed to temptations, and the larger is the measure of grace needed to keep him humble and spiritual; and he will meet with more painful experiences and humbling dispensations. We have little cause to glory in any gifts bestowed on us, or to despise those who have them not. ( [1Cor.12.12-1Cor.12.26] 1Co 12:12-26)
[1Cor.12.12-1Cor.12.26]
Verses 12-26
Christ and his church form one body, as Head and members. Christians become members of this body by baptism. The outward rite is of Divine institution; it is a sign of the new birth, and is called therefore the washing of regeneration, [Titus.3.5] Tit 3:5. But it is by the Spirit, only by the renewing of the Holy Ghost, that we are made members of Christ's body. And by communion with Christ at the Lord's supper, we are strengthened, not by drinking the wine, but by drinking into one Spirit. Each member has its form, place, and use. The meanest makes a part of the body. There must be a distinction of members in the body. So Christ's members have different powers and different places. We should do the duties of our own place, and not murmur, or quarrel with others. All the members of the body are useful and necessary to each other. Nor is there a member of the body of Christ, but may and ought to be useful to fellow-members. As in the natural body of man, the members should be closely united by the strongest bonds of love; the good of the whole should be the object of all. All Christians are dependent one upon another; each is to expect and receive help from the rest. Let us then have more of the spirit of union in our religion.
[1Cor.12.27-1Cor.12.31]
Verses 27-31
Contempt, hatred, envy, and strife, are very unnatural in Christians. It is like the members of the same body being without concern for one another, or quarrelling with each other. The proud, contentious spirit that prevailed, as to spiritual gifts, was thus condemned. The offices and gifts, or favours, dispensed by the Holy Spirit, are noticed. Chief ministers; persons enabled to interpret Scripture; those who laboured in word and doctrine; those who had power to heal diseases; such as helped the sick and weak; such as disposed of the money given in charity by the church, and managed the affairs of the church; and such as could speak divers languages. What holds the last and lowest rank in this list, is the power to speak languages; how vain, if a man does so merely to amuse or to exalt himself! See the distribution of these gifts, not to every one alike, ver. #(29-30). This were to make the church all one, as if the body were all ear, or all eye. The Spirit distributes to every one as he will. We must be content though we are lower and less than others. We must not despise others, if we have greater gifts. How blessed the Christian church, if all the members did their duty! Instead of coveting the highest stations, or the most splendid gifts, let us leave the appointment of his instruments to God, and those in whom he works by his providence. Remember, those will not be approved hereafter who seek the chief places, but those who are most faithful to the trust placed in them, and most diligent in their Master's work.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe necessity and advantage of the grace of love.1–3Its excellency represented by its properties and effects;4–7and by its abiding, and its superiority.8–13
Without love, even great gifts accomplish nothing spiritually (verses 1–3)

The more excellent way mentioned at the end of the previous chapter is love in its fullest meaning, genuine love toward both God and other people.

It is not merely what people commonly call charity—giving money or material goods.

Without this love, even the most impressive spiritual gifts are worthless for the person possessing them and count for nothing in God's sight.

A clear mind and profound learning are of no value spiritually without a loving and generous heart.

Someone may give away money freely and even extravagantly while lacking genuine concern for others.

Doing good to another person brings us no spiritual benefit if we act without love for God and goodwill toward people.

Even giving up all our possessions brings no blessing if our hearts remain withheld from God.

Nor will the most painful suffering earn God's approval in that condition.

How deceived are people who expect acceptance and reward for works that are limited, imperfect, and often corrupted by selfishness!

Christian love is recognizable in its character and actions (verses 4–7)

Paul described the effects of love so that we can examine whether this grace is present in our hearts.

If it is absent, we should not be satisfied until God grants it.

Christian love is evidence of regeneration, a test of our profession of faith in Jesus Christ.

The beautiful description also shows the Corinthian believers how far their actual behavior differed from it.

Love is the enemy of selfishness.

It does not put personal praise, reputation, profit or enjoyment above the good of others.

But this does not mean love destroys every proper concern for our own well-being.

A loving person need not ignore personal needs and legitimate interests.

Rather, love never pursues its own benefit at someone else's expense or by neglecting another person's welfare.

It willingly gives priority to others' needs when required.

How gentle and attractive Christian love is!

How beautiful Christianity would appear to the world if everyone professing it were governed by this divine principle, giving proper attention to the command upon which Christ himself placed such emphasis.

Let us ask ourselves: Does this love live in my heart?

Has it shaped my conduct toward everyone?

Am I willing to abandon selfish ambitions?

We need watchfulness, diligence and prayer.

Love will remain when other gifts pass away (verses 8–13)

Love is more excellent than the impressive gifts the Corinthians admired because it endures.

Love lasts throughout eternity.

Our present knowledge resembles childhood, while the life to come resembles maturity.

How confused and limited a child's understanding appears compared with that of an adult!

When we reach heaven, we will look back upon our best earthly abilities and most valued spiritual gifts with similar recognition of their limitations.

Everything we understand now is dark and incomplete compared with future knowledge.

We see as though through a mirror's reflection or a riddle.

In heaven, however, our knowledge will be freed from confusion and error.

Only heaven's light will remove the clouds that now hide God's face from us.

Love surpasses not only extraordinary spiritual gifts, but even the other central graces—faith and hope.

Faith receives God's revelation and rests upon the divine Redeemer.

Hope looks toward future happiness and waits for it.

But in heaven faith becomes sight and hope becomes enjoyment.

We no longer need to believe that something unseen is true once we see it, or hope for what we already enjoy.

Love, however, becomes perfect.

In heaven we will love God perfectly and love one another perfectly.

What a blessed state, surpassing every earthly comfort!

God is love (1 John 4:8, 16).

Where believers see him face to face as he is, love reaches its greatest height and its full perfection.
classic_reading:
[1Cor.13.1-1Cor.13.3]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
The necessity and advantage of the grace of love. | (1-3) |
Its excellency represented by its properties and effects;
(4-7)
and by its abiding, and its superiority.
(8-13)
Verses 1-3
The excellent way had in view in the close of the former chapter, is not what is meant by charity in our common use of the word, almsgiving, but love in its fullest meaning; true love to God and man. Without this, the most glorious gifts are of no account to us, of no esteem in the sight of God. A clear head and a deep understanding, are of no value without a benevolent and charitable heart. There may be an open and lavish hand, where there is not a liberal and charitable heart. Doing good to others will do none to us, if it be not done from love to God, and good-will to men. If we give away all we have, while we withhold the heart from God, it will not profit. Nor even the most painful sufferings. How are those deluded who look for acceptance and reward for their good works, which are as scanty and defective as they are corrupt and selfish!
[1Cor.13.4-1Cor.13.7]
Verses 4-7
Some of the effects of charity are stated, that we may know whether we have this grace; and that if we have not, we may not rest till we have it. This love is a clear proof of regeneration, and is a touchstone of our professed faith in Christ. In this beautiful description of the nature and effects of love, it is meant to show the Corinthians that their conduct had, in many respects, been a contrast to it. Charity is an utter enemy to selfishness; it does not desire or seek its own praise, or honour, or profit, or pleasure. Not that charity destroys all regard to ourselves, or that the charitable man should neglect himself and all his interests. But charity never seeks its own to the hurt of others, or to neglect others. It ever prefers the welfare of others to its private advantage. How good-natured and amiable is Christian charity! How excellent would Christianity appear to the world, if those who profess it were more under this Divine principle, and paid due regard to the command on which its blessed Author laid the chief stress! Let us ask whether this Divine love dwells in our hearts. Has this principle guided us into becoming behaviour to all men? Are we willing to lay aside selfish objects and aims? Here is a call to watchfulness, diligence, and prayer.
[1Cor.13.8-1Cor.13.13]
Verses 8-13
Charity is much to be preferred to the gifts on which the Corinthians prided themselves. From its longer continuance. It is a grace, lasting as eternity. The present state is a state of childhood, the future that of manhood. Such is the difference between earth and heaven. What narrow views, what confused notions of things, have children when compared with grown men! Thus shall we think of our most valued gifts of this world, when we come to heaven. All things are dark and confused now, compared with what they will be hereafter. They can only be seen as by the reflection in a mirror, or in the description of a riddle; but hereafter our knowledge will be free from all obscurity and error. It is the light of heaven only, that will remove all clouds and darkness that hide the face of God from us. To sum up the excellences of charity, it is preferred not only to gifts, but to other graces, to faith and hope. Faith fixes on the Divine revelation, and assents thereto, relying on the Divine Redeemer. Hope fastens on future happiness, and waits for that; but in heaven, faith will be swallowed up in actual sight, and hope in enjoyment. There is no room to believe and hope, when we see and enjoy. But there, love will be made perfect. There we shall perfectly love God. And there we shall perfectly love one another. Blessed state! how much surpassing the best below! God is love, [1John.4.8] 1Jo 4:8, [1John.4.16] 16. Where God is to be seen as he is, and face to face, there charity is in its greatest height; there only will it be perfected.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesProphecy preferred to the gift of tongues.1–5The unprofitableness of speaking in unknown languages.6–14Exhortations to worship that can be understood.15–25Disorders from vain display of gifts;26–33and from women speaking in the church.34–40
Explaining Scripture is more useful than uninterpreted languages (verses 1–5)

Henry understands prophesying in this passage as explaining Scripture.

Paul compared it with speaking in other languages.

Uninterpreted tongues attracted more attention and more readily gratified spiritual pride.

But they did less to accomplish Christian love's purpose, because they did less to benefit hearers' souls.

No one can be spiritually built up by words they do not understand.

Even the finest teaching accomplishes no good among hearers who cannot speak or understand the language being used.

The value of every ability or possession depends upon how useful it is.

Even sincere religious feeling must be guided by understanding, or it may dishonor the very truths people claim to promote.

Worship without intelligible speech cannot edify (verses 6–14)

Even an apostle could not build up the church if his words were incomprehensible to his hearers.

Speech that communicates no meaning to its audience is like speaking into the air.

The speaker and hearers become foreigners to one another.

The purpose of speech has not been fulfilled.

Christian gatherings should conduct every act of worship in a way that allows everyone to join in and receive spiritual benefit.

Plain, readily understood language is most appropriate for public worship and religious teaching.

A true follower of Christ should care far more about helping others than about earning a reputation for brilliant scholarship or eloquent speaking.

Speak and pray so that hearers understand (verses 15–25)

People cannot sincerely agree with prayers whose meaning they cannot understand.

A faithful gospel minister is far more concerned to benefit other people's souls than to earn public admiration.

That concern shows the minister is Christ's servant.

Children enjoy novelty and unusual displays.

Believers should not imitate that weakness.

We should be like children without malice or deceit, yet mature in our understanding of God's righteousness and ignorant only of the techniques of wrongdoing.

Henry regards it as a fearful judgment when people are led by teachers who force them to worship in an unfamiliar language.

No benefit can come from instruction that is not understood.

If unbelieving visitors enter a church and hear unintelligible preaching or prayer, they may conclude Christianity is absurd.

But when Scripture is clearly explained and the great truths and duties of the gospel are proclaimed, even an unbeliever or someone without formal education may be converted.

God's word may awaken conscience, expose secret sins and move that person to acknowledge their guilt and confess that God truly is present among his people.

Scripture, when clearly and faithfully taught, has extraordinary power to touch the heart.

Orderly worship should build up the whole congregation (verses 26–33)

Public worship should always be governed by one purpose: “Let everything be done for building up.”

If someone speaks in a language unknown to the congregation, another person must be able to interpret it.

Then two miraculous gifts can work together to build up the church and confirm the hearers' faith.

Those explaining Scripture should also speak in an orderly sequence.

Two or three may address a meeting, but not simultaneously.

Someone genuinely inspired by the Spirit of God will show decency and order in delivering what God has revealed.

God never teaches us to neglect our duties or behave in ways unworthy of our age and responsibilities.

Conduct in worship and apostolic instruction (verses 34–40)

Paul urged believing women to seek answers about religious matters from their husbands at home.

Henry draws the lesson that Christian families should gather for spiritual conversation and growth in knowledge.

The Spirit of Christ cannot contradict himself.

Claims of spiritual revelation that contradict the apostle's instruction cannot come from that same Spirit.

Chapter Outline
Prophecy preferred to the gift of tongues. | (1-5) |
The unprofitableness of speaking in unknown languages. | (6-14) |

and from women speaking in the church.

Prophesying, that is, explaining Scripture, is compared with speaking with tongues. What cannot be understood, never can edify. No advantage can be reaped from the most excellent discourses, if delivered in language such as the hearers cannot speak or understand. That cannot answer the end of speaking, which has no meaning; in this case, speaker and hearers are barbarians to each other. All religious services should be so performed in Christian assemblies, that all may join in, and profit by them. Language plain and easy to be understood, is the most proper for public worship, and other religious exercises. Every true follower of Christ will rather desire to do good to others, than to get a name for learning or fine speaking.
[1Cor.14.15-1Cor.14.25]
Verses 15-25

Christians should be like children, void of guile and malice; yet they should not be unskilful as to the word of righteousness, but only as to the arts of mischief. It is a proof that a people are forsaken of God, when he gives them up to the rule of those who teach them to worship in another language. They can never be benefitted by such teaching. Yet thus the preachers did who delivered their instructions in an unknown tongue. His conscience might be touched, the secrets of his heart might be revealed to him, and so he might be brought to confess his guilt, and to own that God was present in the assembly. When the apostle exhorts Christian women to seek information on religious subjects from their husbands at home, it shows that believing families ought to assemble for promoting spiritual knowledge. The Spirit of Christ can never contradict itself; and if their revelations are against those of the apostle, they do not come from the same Spirit. The way to keep peace, truth, and order in the church, is to seek that which is good for it, to bear with that which is not hurtful to its welfare, and to keep up good behaviour, order, and decency.

Henry argues that the philosophers' teachings offer nothing comparable to the doctrine Paul proclaims.

A person who abandons the gospel's faith has believed in vain.

Christ's resurrection was foretold in the Old Testament Scriptures.

Many witnesses saw him after he rose.

God can convert sinners into saints by grace and use the memory of their past sins to make them humble, diligent and faithful.

Paul attributed everything good within him to the grace of God.

True Christians can recognize what God has done for them, in them and through them, yet also see how far they remain from their duty.

They therefore regard themselves humbly before the Lord.

All the apostles agreed upon the central testimony: Jesus Christ was crucified and rose from the dead.

This is the heart of Christian faith.

In this truth they lived and died.

Denying resurrection makes Christian hope empty (verses 12–19)

Paul had established that Christ rose.

He now answered those denying the future resurrection of the body.

If Christ had not risen, there could have been no effective justification or salvation.

Faith in someone still held by death would be empty.

The resurrection of Jesus is the proof of our future bodily resurrection.

Even believers who died trusting Christ would have perished in their sins if he had never risen.

If resurrection and future reward were impossible, every Christian hope would be confined to this life alone.

Then believers, especially under the persecution experienced in the apostles' day, would be more miserable than other people.

But this is not their actual condition.

Christ's people possess solid comfort and hope even amid severe trials and persecution.

Christ's victory guarantees resurrection to those united to him (verses 20–34)

Everyone joined to Christ through faith has a secure promise of resurrection through his rising from the dead.

Through the first Adam's sin, the human race became mortal and inherited fallen nature.

Through Christ's resurrection, everyone brought into the spiritual life of his people by the Holy Spirit will rise and live forever.

There is an order in the resurrection.

Christ himself is the firstfruits.

At his coming, his redeemed people will rise.

Henry says the wicked will also rise later, and then this present order of things will come to its end.

If we wish to triumph on that day, we must now submit to Christ's rule, receive his salvation and live for his glory.

The completion of Christ's saving work will bring all glory to God, and his people will serve and enjoy him forever.

Paul mentions people “baptized for the dead.”

The meaning is not certain.

Henry suggests as one possibility that baptism here figuratively means suffering, persecution or martyrdom, as in Matthew 20:22–23.

He asks what would become of people who suffered terrible injuries or lost their lives for faith in resurrection if the dead never rose.

Whatever Paul meant, the Corinthian readers evidently understood his argument.

Without resurrection and eternal life, the suffering required by Christian faith would have no promised reward.

But we are not animals who simply live and die without a future.

Failure to believe in resurrection and the life to come reveals ignorance of God.

Recognizing God's existence and Providence, and seeing the many injustices of this life—where good people often suffer most—should lead us to expect a future state in which matters will be put right.

Avoid close fellowship with people who encourage ungodliness.

Warn children and young people especially to avoid corrupting companionship.

Awaken to righteousness and stop sinning.

First, how can dead people rise? By what power and means?

Second, what kind of bodies will they possess? Will they have exactly the same shape, size, organs and qualities?

Henry distinguishes the first as an objection from those opposing resurrection and the second as a question from curious but doubtful minds.

God's almighty power answers the first.

Each year we see a partial analogy in grain sown into the ground and springing into life.

It is foolish to deny that God's power can raise the dead while we see him continually bringing life from what appears dead.

As to the second question, grain changes greatly when it grows, and resurrected bodies will also be transformed.

We do not fully understand how life arises from a seed.

God's ordinary works of creation and Providence should humble us as well as lead us to admire him.

Different kinds of plants and earthly bodies vary.

So do the heavenly bodies and their glories.

Burial resembles placing seed in the ground so that it may spring up later.

The gospel reveals many truths that earlier generations did not clearly know.

Chapter 15
Chapter Outline
The apostle proves the resurrection of Christ from the dead.
(1-11)
Those answered who deny the resurrection of the body.
(12-19)
The resurrection of believers to eternal life.
(20-34)
Objections against it answered.

The mystery of the change that will be made on those living at Christ's second coming.
(51-54)
The believer's triumph over death and the grave, An exhortation to diligence.
(55-58)
Verses 1-11
The word resurrection, usually points out our existence beyond the grave. Of the apostle's doctrine not a trace can be found in all the teaching of philosophers. The doctrine of Christ's death and resurrection, is the foundation of Christianity. Remove this, and all our hopes for eternity sink at once. And it is by holding this truth firm, that Christians stand in the day of trial, and are kept faithful to God. We believe in vain, unless we keep in the faith of the gospel. This truth is confirmed by Old Testament prophecies; and many saw Christ after he was risen. This apostle was highly favoured, but he always had a low opinion of himself, and expressed it. When sinners are, by Divine grace, turned into saints, God causes the remembrance of former sins to make them humble, diligent, and faithful. He ascribes to Divine grace all that was valuable in him. True believers, though not ignorant of what the Lord has done for, in, and by them, yet when they look at their whole conduct and their obligations, they are led to feel that none are so worthless as they are. All true Christians believe that Jesus Christ, and him crucified, and then risen from the dead, is the sun and substance of Christianity. All the apostles agreed in this testimony; by this faith they lived, and in this faith they died.
[1Cor.15.12-1Cor.15.19]
Verses 12-19
Having shown that Christ was risen, the apostle answers those who said there would be no resurrection. There had been no justification, or salvation, if Christ had not risen. And must not faith in Christ be vain, and of no use, if he is still among the dead? The proof of the resurrection of the body is the resurrection of our Lord. Even those who died in the faith, had perished in their sins, if Christ had not risen. All who believe in Christ, have hope in him, as a Redeemer; hope for redemption and salvation by him; but if there is no resurrection, or future recompence, their hope in him can only be as to this life. And they must be in a worse condition than the rest of mankind, especially at the time, and under the circumstances, in which the apostles wrote; for then Christians were hated and persecuted by all men. But it is not so; they, of all men, enjoy solid comforts amidst all their difficulties and trials, even in the times of the sharpest persecution.
[1Cor.15.20-1Cor.15.34]
Verses 20-34
All that are by faith united to Christ, are by his resurrection assured of their own. As through the sin of the first Adam, all men became mortal, because all had from him the same sinful nature, so, through the resurrection of Christ, shall all who are made to partake of the Spirit, and the spiritual nature, revive, and live for ever. There will be an order in the resurrection. Christ himself has been the first-fruits; at his coming, his redeemed people will be raised before others; at the last the wicked will rise also. Then will be the end of this present state of things. Would we triumph in that solemn and important season, we must now submit to his rule, accept his salvation, and live to his glory. Then shall we rejoice in the completion of his undertaking, that God may receive the whole glory of our salvation, that we may for ever serve him, and enjoy his favour. What shall those do, who are baptized for the dead, if the dead rise not at all? Perhaps baptism is used here in a figure, for afflictions, sufferings, and martyrdom, as [Matt.20.22] Mt 20:22, [Matt.20.23] 23. What is, or will become of those who have suffered many and great injuries, and have even lost their lives, for this doctrine of the resurrection, if the dead rise not at all? Whatever the meaning may be, doubtless the apostle's argument was understood by the Corinthians. And it is as plain to us that Christianity would be a foolish profession, if it proposed advantage to themselves by their faithfulness to God; and to have our fruit to holiness, that our end may be everlasting life. But we must not live like beasts, as we do not die like them. It must be ignorance of God that leads any to disbelieve the resurrection and future life. Those who own a God and a providence, and observe how unequal things are in the present life, how frequently the best men fare worst, cannot doubt as to an after-state, where every thing will be set to rights. Let us not be joined with ungodly men; but warn all around us, especially children and young persons, to shun them as a pestilence. Let us awake to righteousness, and not sin.
[1Cor.15.35-1Cor.15.50]
Verses 35-50
1. How are the dead raised up? that is, by what means? How can they be raised? 2. As to the bodies which shall rise. Will it be with the like shape, and form, and stature, and members, and qualities? The former objection is that of those who opposed the doctrine, the latter of curious doubters. To the first the answer is, This was to be brought about by Divine power; that power which all may see does somewhat like it, year after year, in the death and revival of the corn. It is foolish to question the Almighty power of God to raise the dead, when we see it every day quickening and reviving things that are dead. To the second inquiry; The grain undergoes a great change; and so will the dead, when they rise and live again. The seed dies, though a part of it springs into new life, though how it is we cannot fully understand. The works of creation and providence daily teach us to be humble, as well as to admire the Creator's wisdom and goodness. There is a great variety among other bodies, as there is among plants. There is a variety of glory among heavenly bodies. The bodies of the dead, when they rise, will be fitted for the heavenly bodies. The bodies of the dead, when they rise, will be fitted for the heavenly state; and there will be a variety of glories among them. Burying the dead, is like committing seed to the earth, that it may spring out of it again. Nothing is more loathsome than a dead body. But believers shall at the resurrection have bodies, made fit to be for ever united with spirits made perfect. To God all things are possible. He is the Author and Source of spiritual life and holiness, unto all his people, by the supply of his Holy Spirit to the soul; and he will also quicken and change the body by his Spirit. The dead in Christ shall not only rise, but shall rise thus gloriously changed. The bodies of the saints, when they rise again, will be changed. They will be then glorious and spiritual bodies, fitted to the heavenly world and state, where they are ever afterwards to dwell. The human body in its present form, and with its wants and weaknesses, cannot enter or enjoy the kingdom of God. Then let us not sow to the flesh, of which we can only reap corruption. And the body follows the state of the soul. He, therefore, who neglects the life of the soul, casts away his present good; he who refuses to live to God, squanders all he has.
[1Cor.15.51-1Cor.15.58]
Verses 51-58
All the saints should not die, but all would be changed. In the gospel, many truths, before hidden in mystery, are made known. Death never shall appear in the regions to which our Lord will bear his risen saints. Therefore let us seek the full assurance of faith and hope, that in the midst of pain, and in the prospect of death, we may think calmly on the horrors of the tomb; assured that our bodies will there sleep, and in the mean time our souls will be present with the Redeemer. Sin gives death all its hurtful power. The sting of death is sin; but Christ, by dying, has taken out this sting; he has made atonement for sin, he has obtained remission of it. The strength of sin is the law. None can answer its demands, endure its curse, or do away his own transgressions. Hence terror and anguish. And hence death is terrible to the unbelieving and the impenitent. Death may seize a believer, but it cannot hold him in its power. How many springs of joy to the saints, and of thanksgiving to God, are opened by the death and resurrection, the sufferings and conquests of the Redeemer! In verse #(58), we have an exhortation, that believers should be stedfast, firm in the faith of that gospel which the apostle preached, and they received. Also, to be unmovable in their hope and expectation of this great privilege, of being raised incorruptible and immortal. And to abound in the work of the Lord, always doing the Lord's service, and obeying the Lord's commands. May Christ give us faith, and increase our faith, that we may not only be safe, but joyful and triumphant.

The collection for believers in Jerusalem (verses 1–9)

Good examples from other Christians and congregations ought to encourage us toward generous action.

It is wise to set aside resources for good purposes.

Those rich in the present world should be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

Diligence alone will not make anyone prosperous without God's blessing (Proverbs 10:4, 22).

What better encouragement toward charity for God's people than remembering that everything we possess is God's gift?

Acts of mercy are genuine fruit of love for God and are appropriate ways of serving him on the Lord's Day.

Ministers carry out their proper work when they encourage and assist efforts of charity.

A Christian minister should remain concerned for the people among whom he has worked faithfully and fruitfully for a long time.

Every plan should be made with submission to God's Providence (James 4:15).

Opposition and enemies do not necessarily discourage faithful, successful ministers.

Such difficulty may instead increase their zeal and courage.

They are often more troubled by the hardness of their hearers' hearts and the backsliding of professing Christians than by attacks from outsiders.

Timothy and Apollos should receive honorable treatment (verses 10–12)

Timothy was doing the Lord's work.

Therefore, to needlessly trouble him was to grieve the Holy Spirit, and to despise him was to dishonor the One who sent him.

Those engaged in Christ's work deserve kindness, respect and consideration.

Faithful ministers should not compete through jealousy.

They should protect one another's reputation and usefulness and show sincere concern for one another's welfare.

Watchfulness, firmness and active love (verses 13–18)

A Christian is always exposed to spiritual danger.

Therefore, believers must remain watchful, established in the gospel's faith and unwilling to abandon it.

Faith in Christ alone enables them to stand firm when temptation comes.

But Christian courage must always be accompanied by love governing the heart and visible in conduct.

There is a great difference between steadfastness in Christ and agitated, uncontrolled excitement.

Paul commended some people who served Christ and cared for the church.

Those who serve believers, protect the churches' honor and help remove unjust reproaches deserve grateful respect and love.

The Corinthians should willingly recognize everyone who worked with Paul and assisted him in his service.

Greetings and final appeal to love Christ (verses 19–24)

Christianity does not abolish courtesy.

True religion encourages kind, considerate and helpful behavior toward everyone.

People who use their faith as an excuse for bitter, unfriendly conduct misrepresent Christianity.

Christian greetings should not be empty compliments.

They express real goodwill and ask God's grace and blessing upon others.

Every Christian household should resemble a small Christian church.

Where two or three gather in Christ's name and he is present among them, there is a church.

Paul ends with a solemn warning.

Many people constantly pronounce Christ's name without genuinely loving him in their hearts.

No one sincerely loves Christ while refusing his commands or despising his law.

Some people are Christian in name only.

They do not love Jesus Christ the Lord sincerely and therefore do not belong to God's people or enjoy his favor.

Whoever does not love the Lord Jesus Christ remains without the remedy of salvation.

Let us never be satisfied with religious profession alone.

Ask whether we possess love for Christ, desire for his salvation, gratitude for his mercy and obedience to his commands.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ contains every good gift needed for this life and eternity.

Wishing that grace upon a friend is wishing the greatest possible good.

We cannot desire anything better, and we should not desire anything less for our brothers and sisters in Christ.

True Christianity makes us seek the blessings of both worlds for those we love.

Paul had spoken plainly and rebuked the Corinthians' faults with necessary severity.

But he departed in love, affirming his affection for them in Christ.

May our love be with everyone who belongs to Christ Jesus.

Examine yourselves.

Do all things seem worthless when compared with Christ and his righteousness?

Do you knowingly indulge some sin or neglect a duty you know God requires?

Such serious and honest questions help reveal the spiritual condition of our souls.

[1Cor.16.13-1Cor.16.18]

By this faith alone he will be able to keep his ground in an hour of temptation. Christians should be careful that charity not only reigns in their hearts, but shines in their lives. There is a great difference between Christian firmness and feverish warmth and transport. The apostle gave particular directions as to some who served the cause of Christ among them. Those who serve the saints, those who desire the honour of the churches, and to remove reproaches from them, are to be thought much of, and loved.
